slides.title: They didn't change the product. They changed the map.
slides.brief: Ultra-realistic business case study infographic, clean white background with subtle blue-grey tonal depth. The dominant element is a large, professionally rendered line graph occupying the CENTER 70% of the slide — styled like a McKinsey or BCG case exhibit. X-axis: years from 2000 to 2007. Y-axis: Volume Index (100 = baseline). The line starts at 100 in 2000, grows modestly to 115 by 2002, then visibly flattens — a near-horizontal plateau from 2002 to 2003, the line nearly dead flat. Then at 2003, a sharp annotation marker drops from the top: a bold vertical dotted line labeled in a clean callout box: "GO-TO-MARKET TRANSFORMATION LAUNCHED" with a small sub-label: "Tier 2 & Tier 3 mapping. Distributor networks rebuilt." From 2003, the line breaks sharply upward at a steep angle — climbing aggressively through 2004, 2005, 2006, ending at 400 on the Y-axis by 2007. The area under the post-2003 curve is filled with a soft blue gradient. At the 2007 endpoint, a large bold callout bubble: "4X VOLUME" in massive dark type. The plateau section of the line is colored red and annotated: "Tier 1 saturation". The growth section is colored electric blue. Below the graph, a thin dark rule, then a three-column insight strip: "DECISION:" "Go deeper, not wider" | "METHOD:" "Tier 2 & Tier 3 market mapping" | "RESULT:" "4x volume in five years". At the top of the slide in bold dark condensed: "THEY DIDN'T CHANGE THE PRODUCT. THEY CHANGED THE MAP." Looks like a real HBR case study exhibit — data-precise, visually undeniable.

slides.title: Every category has fallen. One hasn't.
slides.brief: Ultra-realistic editorial infographic render, stark white background with a faint cool grey paper texture — like a premium financial publication spread. The dominant element is a thick black horizontal timeline bar running the full width of the slide at the vertical center, with precise year markers notched below it: 2010, 2012, 2014, 2016, 2018, 2020, 2022, 2024, 2025. Above the timeline, at each conquered year, sits a meticulously rendered miniature tombstone — dark grey granite, beveled edges, slightly weathered — each with a clean serif RIP engraving and a category label beneath it in small tight caps: "EMAIL — RIP 2016 / Killed by: GPT Mail", "DOCUMENTS — RIP 2018 / Killed by: Notion AI", "SPREADSHEETS — RIP 2020 / Killed by: Excel Copilot", "CODE — RIP 2022 / Killed by: GitHub Copilot", "SCHEDULING — RIP 2023 / Killed by: Reclaim AI", "CRM — RIP 2024 / Killed by: Salesforce Einstein." Each tombstone casts a precise short shadow downward. The tombstones increase slightly in size left to right, building visual momentum. At the far right end of the timeline — 2025 — the tombstone is missing. In its place: a single blinking red cursor, hovering above the timeline on a clean white pedestal block. Beside the cursor, a category label in bold red type: "PRESENTATIONS." No RIP. No date. Just the cursor, blinking. Below the timeline, a thin dark rule separator, then in small precise sans-serif across the full width: "Five categories disrupted. One remains. The cursor is blinking." At the top of the slide in massive bold dark condensed typography: "EVERY CATEGORY HAS FALLEN. ONE HASN'T." Subtext in smaller grey italic beneath: "AI didn't forget presentations. It just hasn't arrived yet." Print-precise linework. Zero decorative noise. McKinsey-cold editorial finish.
